tip: Think of it as the middle room of the chest, with the lungs as the walls on either side.
Peri- means around and cardio means heart, so the name tells you exactly where it sits.
The tough outer bag. It is strong enough to stop the heart overfilling, which is why it does not stretch much.
Epi- means upon, so this is the layer sitting directly on the muscle. It is the same sheet as the visceral pericardium.
Myo- means muscle, so this is the thick middle layer that does the actual pumping.
Endo- means within. It lines the chambers and is continuous with the lining of the blood vessels leaving the heart.
Blood coming back from the body arrives here first. Atria are the thin-walled receiving rooms, not the pumps.
It only has to push blood as far as the lungs, so its wall is noticeably thinner than its partner on the left.
The only chamber that receives blood already carrying oxygen, arriving from the lungs.
The thickest wall of the four chambers, because it has to push blood all the way around the body.
Septum means a dividing wall, and inter-ventricular tells you which two rooms it divides.
Three cusps, and it sits on the right. A common way to keep it straight: tri before bi, right before left.
Two cusps, on the left. It is named for a bishop's mitre, which has the same two-flap shape.
Guards the way out to the lungs. Semilunar means half-moon, which is the shape of each of its three pockets.
The last gate blood passes through on its way to the body. Its cusps fill like pockets to snap it shut.
Often called heart strings. They stop the valve flaps blowing inside out when the ventricle squeezes.
The little mounds that anchor the heart strings. They tighten just before the ventricle does, taking up the slack.
The one artery that carries blood low in oxygen. It leaves the right side and splits to both lungs.
The body's largest artery, arching over the heart like a walking stick before heading down the trunk.
Superior means above, so this is the one draining the head, neck and arms.
Inferior means below, so this one drains everything south of the diaphragm. It is the larger of the pair.
They branch off the aorta almost immediately, so the heart feeds itself first before anything else gets blood.
The drain, not the supply. It collects used blood from the heart wall and empties into the right atrium.
A hole in the wall between the atria, open only before birth so blood can skip the lungs.
The dimple left behind after that fetal opening seals up. Fossa means a shallow pit.
